name: PT Intra Golflink Resorts Tbk

frontmatter.title: Intra Golflink Resorts — a fair-valued land bank inside a low-return operating company
frontmatter.summary: GOLF owns three golf courses and a township land bank carried at appraised value, but earns a negligible return on it and converts almost nothing into free cash. Our valuation adds the Belitung associate at book and the appraised land at a stated probability of a value-realising transaction, and the result still sits far below the price. Initiate at SELL.
thesis: The accounts are not wrong that the land is worth what it says; the problem is that a minority shareholder owns cash flows, not hectares, and those cash flows earn a sub-one-percent return on the revalued asset base.
{'Nine-month revenue growth is real but narrow': 'all of it is property handover timing against flat golf revenue and a shrinking restaurant line.'}
Reported free cash flow was positive only before the development programme and has been negative since, because capex has run at three-quarters to one-and-a-quarter times revenue [S0][S3].
The controlling family holds almost the entire register and the free float must rise to the regulatory minimum within a transition window, which points to future supply of shares, not demand.
Even our bull case, which assumes five points more growth and two points more margin, values the equity below today's price.

Annual general meeting — dividend declaration and any free-float corporate action
Banyan Tree boutique hotel at New Kuta Golf scheduled for completion
End of the three-year IDX transition window to reach the minimum free float

blocks.text: **SELL · target Rp46 · total expected return -60.4% including forecast dividends · price Rp116**

We initiate coverage of PT Intra Golflink Resorts at SELL. The company owns and operates three golf courses — Palm Hill in Sentul, New Kuta in Pecatu, Bali, and Black Rocks in Belitung — and develops residential lots around them [S7]. It is controlled by Hutomo Mandala Putra through PT Bali Pecatu Graha, which holds 88.5% of the shares; with a second family vehicle holding a small stake, the public float is 10.0% [S5].

The investment question is not whether the land is valuable. It is. The group carries fixed assets of roughly IDR7,266.0bn against annual revenue of IDR215.5bn, and the revaluation surplus inside equity is 6,898 IDR bn [S3][S4]. The question is what a minority shareholder can claim from that land. On our numbers, very little: net profit of IDR51.8bn on equity of IDR8,018.8bn is a return of about 0.6% [S3]. Reported operating cash flow was IDR44.2bn in the last financial year against capex of IDR165.8bn, so reported free cash flow was negative [S3]; it was positive in FY2022 and FY2023, before the development programme began, and has been negative since [S0].

**Where we differ from the market.** The shares trade at 0.3x times book, a discount that looks like a bargain until you notice that book is mostly an appraisal, not capital anyone put in. Strip out the revaluation surplus and the market is paying roughly twice the capital that was actually invested, for a business earning a mid-single-digit return on that capital. The market is paying a steep discount to the appraised land — the whole company is capitalised at IDR2,260.5bn against land alone carried at IDR6.62tn [S0][S7] — but it is still paying several times what the cash flows on that land support. Our view is the same in both places: the operating business is worth what it generates, and the land is worth the appraised value only to a buyer who can transact, which a minority cannot compel. We therefore credit the land route explicitly and at a stated probability in the valuation bridge rather than leaving it out of the base case or pretending the market is close to it. What we do not think is worth the price is the probability the market attaches to a full-value land realisation, given that the pace of monetisation is set by absorption in Sentul and Pecatu rather than by the size of the land bank, and that the family, not the minority, decides when to sell.

**What moves the value.** Three things. First, the pace of property handovers: nine-month revenue rose 21.5% on a real-estate line that quadrupled against a very weak comparable, while golf revenue was flat [S4][S6]. Second, capex: the moment development spending falls back toward maintenance, free cash flow turns, and our forecast has that happening from the coming year as construction completes [S4]. Third, the free-float fix, which will be met with new shares or a sale by the controller, and which is the largest per-share risk in the name [S5].

**Why SELL and not HOLD.** Our three methods land between the P/E cross-check at Rp29 and the EV/EBITDA cross-check at Rp48, and our bull scenario — five points more revenue growth, two points more gross margin and a faster capex fade — still produces Rp75 against a price of Rp116 [S0][S3][S4]. When the most favourable of our scenarios is below the market price, the rating is not a close call. The stock can of course rise: it is illiquid, it has fallen a long way from its listing price, and a single large handover quarter can transform a reported year [S6]. That is volatility, not value.

Small-cap property-and-leisure names in Indonesia habitually trade below appraised net asset value because control is concentrated, disclosure is thin and there is no mechanism for a minority holder to force a sale of the underlying land. Investors who buy them are usually buying a catalyst — a strategic buyer, a restructuring, a change of control — rather than a stream of cash flow. Where no such catalyst exists, the discount can persist for a decade.

GOLF is a golf-course owner-operator that has been recast as a destination developer. It was founded under the name PT Dreamland Pecatu Golf, renamed PT Intra Golflink Resorts in 2005, and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in July 2024 at an offer price of Rp200 per share [S6][S7]. It reports four segments: golf, restaurant, real estate and other [S3].

The golf business operates three eighteen-hole courses: New Kuta Golf on 85.0 hectares in Pecatu, Bali; Palm Hill Golf Club at Sentul in Bogor, West Java; and Black Rocks Hotel & Golf Club on 72.2 hectares in Belitung, which is held through the associate PT Belitung Golf and Resorts rather than consolidated line by line [S7]. Revenue comes from green fees and cart fees, driving-range ball sales, membership, equipment rental, tournaments and on-course food and beverage [S7]. This is the recurring core: it generated 102 IDR bn of segment revenue in the last financial year, or just over half the group total, at a segment operating margin in the high twenties [S3][S4].

The restaurant segment runs the clubhouse and beach food-and-beverage outlets, including the Laskar Pelangi Beach Food Plaza in Belitung [S7]. It is the weakest business in the group: revenue fell year on year in the first nine months of the current year and the segment earns a low-single-digit operating margin [S4].

The real-estate segment is where the growth and the argument live. The group sells land parcels, residential units and commercial property, principally through a joint operation with PT Perintis Triniti Properti for the Sequoia Hills township at Sentul — 76.0 hectares, fourteen clusters of which four have been marketed [S7]. Under that cooperation agreement the Sentul land is committed to the joint operation, and parcels of non-golf land have been sold under binding sale agreements [S4]. In the last financial year real estate produced 79.4 IDR bn of revenue and 35.0 IDR bn of segment operating income, making it the largest single profit pool in the group despite being the second-largest line by revenue [S3]. Alongside it the group is developing The Links Golf Villa in Bali and a Banyan Tree boutique hotel on 5.1 hectares at New Kuta [S7].

**Footprint and position.** This is a challenger, not a leader. Indonesia has more than 180 active golf courses, and GOLF's three are premium destination courses rather than a national network [S7]. Its advantage is location: Pecatu is one of the most sought-after clifftop addresses in Bali, Sentul is an established affluent exurb of Jakarta, and Belitung is a government-promoted tourism destination. Its disadvantage is that all three sit on land carried at appraised value, which raises the return hurdle the operating business must clear.

**Group and control.** The company is a subsidiary of PT Bali Pecatu Graha, the vehicle of Hutomo Mandala Putra, and the president commissioner is Darma Mangkuluhur Hutomo [S7]. PT Bali Pecatu Graha holds 88.5% and a second family vehicle holds a small stake, leaving 10.0% in public hands [S5]. The group employs about 155.0 people directly, which tells you how capital-intensive and how thinly staffed the operating business is relative to its asset base [S0].

**Strategy.** Management states its intention to convert from a course operator into an integrated golf, hospitality and property destination business, and to monetise its extensive land bank for recurring income [S7]. In practice the strategy is to use golf as the anchor that makes adjacent residential plots sellable, and to add hotel rooms that raise the value of both. That is a coherent model — it is the model every successful golf-resort developer runs — but it is capital-hungry and slow, and it explains why the accounts show large assets and small profits.

A golf-resort developer typically earns most of its return from the residential land around the course rather than from the course itself. The course is a marketing asset that justifies a price premium on plots; the plots are the product. This is why course operators so often become property developers, and why their reported returns depend on plot absorption rather than on green fees.

**Size and growth.** The company's own annual report, citing the Indonesian Golf Course Owners Association, puts the number of active courses above 180 courses and describes player numbers as having risen by roughly a third over five years, driven by outdoor-sport trends and golf tourism into Bali, Bintan, Batam and Lombok [S7]. The same report cites a market study projecting Indonesian golf market growth accelerating from 11.6% in the first year of the forecast to just over fourteen per cent by the end of the decade [S7]. We treat that projection as a company-cited market estimate rather than an independent forecast, but the direction is corroborated by the two things that matter most for this name: inbound tourism into Bali and the regional pricing gap.

**The pricing gap is the structural driver.** Indonesian green fees are quoted in the company's report as up to around seventy per cent cheaper than comparable regional destinations such as Singapore and Malaysia [S7]. For a Bali course with international-standard design, that is a durable cost advantage in the regional golf-tourism market, and it is the strongest single argument for the golf business's long-run volume. It is also why the golf line should be able to grow at or above Indonesian nominal output without taking share from anyone.

**The property market is the constraint.** The company cites central-bank data showing residential property sales growing in the high single digits year on year, with small houses strong, mid-sized houses modest and large houses still contracting [S7]. GOLF's Sequoia Hills product sits at the premium end of a market where the premium end is the weak segment. That is the most important industry fact for our forecast: the land bank is large, but the addressable demand for the houses built on it is in the part of the market that is shrinking, not growing.

**Moat.** We score the moat as narrow. The mechanisms that would justify a wide moat are present in part — location scarcity in Pecatu is genuine and cannot be replicated; the installed base of members creates some switching cost; and the course-plus-residence bundle is a real product differentiator. But there is no evidence that any of these is widening. Golf revenue was flat year on year over nine months while the group added holes and facilities, which is what a business without pricing power looks like [S4][S6]. A moat that does not show up in realised price is a claim, not a finding.

**Five forces.** Rivalry is moderate and local: three courses in three distinct catchments against a fragmented national field. Barriers to entry are high for a new championship course — land, permitting and water — and low for a new residential development nearby, which caps the property margin. Supplier power is low, except for water and land, both politically sensitive in Bali. Buyer power is high in property and rising in golf, because the customer is a discretionary spender with many regional alternatives. Substitutes are the real threat: any leisure spend competes with travel, and the domestic golfer has cheaper municipal options [S7]. The net effect is a business that should earn a normal return in a good year and a poor one in a bad year, which is roughly what the record shows.

**External influences.** Three matter. The rupiah: the group reports in rupiah and its Bali customers are substantially foreign, so a weaker rupiah helps inbound golf tourism while raising the cost of imported course and hotel equipment [S4]. Interest rates: the property business is rate-sensitive and the house macro desk is cautious on Indonesian rate-sensitive domestic demand. Tourism policy and access: Bali arrivals, visa rules and flight capacity set the ceiling on the New Kuta and Banyan Tree economics.

Golf is one of the more water-intensive leisure land uses per hectare, and the southern Balinese resorts have faced repeated drought stress and groundwater regulation. A course licence to operate is therefore a political asset as much as a physical one, and course closures for water reasons are not unheard of in the region.

**What the reported numbers actually say.** Revenue grew from IDR177.6bn to IDR215.5bn over the two years to the last financial year, but the composition shifted hard toward property. In the last financial year golf produced 102 IDR bn, real estate 79.4 IDR bn, restaurant 24.1 IDR bn and other businesses the balance [S3]. Nine months into the current year revenue is 133 IDR bn, up 21.5%, of which golf is 77.7 IDR bn and real estate 31.9 IDR bn [S4][S6]. Read those lines together and the story is clear: golf is flat, restaurant is shrinking, and the entire increase is property handover timing concentrated in the second half. Our FY2026E growth of 11.0% is below the nine-month rate for exactly that reason: last year's December quarter carried just under half of FY2025 revenue, so a straight repeat of that quarter's handover value is what lands the year at our rate [S3][S4]. We hold the fourth quarter flat rather than assume it grows again: neither the annual report nor the nine-month accounts disclose unbilled sales or a handover pipeline, and a quarter up about a tenth on last year's would be needed to reach a mid-teens year. The base case does not credit that.

**The earnings-quality flag that matters most is depreciation.** The data pack carries depreciation of IDR3.1bn for the last financial year because it captured only the general-and-administrative allocation. The financial statements show total depreciation of 17.8 IDR bn, most of which sits inside cost of revenues — the allocation to cost of revenues is the larger line and the administration charge is the smaller one [S3]. The pack figure and the total are not two estimates of the same thing: the pack read the smaller of the two allocations, so its depreciation is roughly a sixth of the real charge. Restating this takes EBITDA to IDR83.4bn and leaves earnings before interest and tax unchanged, because the charge was always being taken. Every cash-flow and leverage conclusion in this report rests on the restated figure. We have made the same restatement for the prior year, which the note puts at 16.1 IDR bn [S3].

**Margins and costs.** Gross margin was 59.9% in the last financial year. Over the nine months to September, gross profit was IDR73.4bn on revenue of IDR133.2bn, a margin in the mid-fifties — the difference from the full year is mix, because property lots carry a lower gross margin than green fees [S3][S4]. That is not a deterioration in the golf business; it is arithmetic. The forward input, which is a forecast and not a reported figure, is 55.5% for the current year rising to 56.0% by the end of the explicit forecast as golf and hotel revenue mix back in [S0]. Operating expenses are the heavier problem, though the direction has improved: general and administrative costs were IDR40.3bn in the first nine months against IDR35.2bn a year earlier, growth well below the 21.5% revenue increase, so operating leverage is beginning to show even with a fixed club overhead across three sites and about 155.0 employees [S0][S4]. Our forecast assumes that modest operating leverage continues — the expense ratio drifts down as revenue scales — but no cost programme, because none has been announced.

**Cash flow and capex.** This is the crux. Capex was 313 IDR bn in the year before last, 166 IDR bn in the last financial year, and 165 IDR bn in the first nine months of the current year [S3][S4]. The reported cash flow is unambiguous: operating cash flow of 44.2 IDR bn against capex of IDR165.8bn left free cash flow negative [S3]. The group is not maintaining three golf courses; it is building a hotel, adding holes and putting in township infrastructure, with buildings under construction roughly half complete and landscape almost finished, and completion scheduled over the next two years [S4]. Our forecast runs capex at one hundred per cent of revenue this year, fading to 15.0% by the end of the explicit forecast and to 15.0% in terminal — above D&A at 9.5%, because the tail is set to the commissioning schedule and the build-out of the committed pipeline, not to a land-purchase programme: FY2025 land additions were nil and inventory land under development fell, so there is no sourced recurring land-acquisition spend to carry [S4]. That fade is the largest assumption in the model, and the risk to our target is two-sided: a faster fade raises value, a slower one cuts it hard.

**Working capital and the balance sheet.** Net working capital of IDR435.9bn looks alarming against revenue until the components are separated. Real-estate inventory held for development and other receivables from related parties of 195 IDR bn make up most of it [S4]. The receivable is financing extended to affiliated entities and its collection has not been evidenced, so we credit it at zero: we strip it out of operating working capital and we do not add it to the bridge. That is a deliberate, single treatment — the model does not hold it at book anywhere. More importantly, the last financial year proves the inventory does not convert: net working capital fell from IDR750.5bn to IDR435.9bn, a release that should have lifted operating cash flow, yet reported operating cash flow was only IDR44.2bn [S3]. The release went into other assets, including the related-party receivable, not into cash. We therefore start the forecast at the FY2025 ratio less the receivable and release working capital only slowly, after FY2028, ending at a level that assumes the developer sells land without fully replenishing it; FY2025 land additions were nil, so we do not fund a land-buying programme the filings do not show [S3][S4]. Balance-sheet risk is not low: cash of IDR156.7bn at 30 September against bank loans of IDR475.5bn, with free cash flow negative [S4]. The concentration is on the debt side: the loans are one Bank Nationalnobu facility [S4 p.49], while the cash is spread across Nationalnobu, BNI, Mandiri, BCA, BSI and BPD Bali [S4 p.34]. The company's own gearing note of IDR93.3bn is a third definition — total liabilities less cash — and is not comparable with net bank debt, which is why the model's FY2025 net debt line and the gearing note differ [S3].

**Interest and the capitalisation tail.** The bank facility costs 11.0% a year [S4]. Nine-month finance expense was marginal against that rate because interest on the hotel under construction is capitalised into the asset [S4]. We carry the contractual rate from the first forecast year, so our FY2026E interest charge of IDR50.0bn runs well above the current cash charge: that is the rate that applies once the hotel is commissioned in 2027-28, and we prefer it in the forecast to letting capitalisation flatter near-term earnings.

**Capital allocation.** The record is a twenty per cent dividend payout — 13.5 IDR bn paid in the middle of last year and a similar amount this year — funded while free cash flow was negative and cash was falling [S3][S7]. That is a defensible signal to the market, and it is also money that did not go into the development pipeline. We model the payout unchanged because management has given no indication of a change, but note that a company with negative free cash flow paying a dividend is either confident about the pipeline or managing its share price.

**Returns on capital.** Return on equity is 0.6% [S0]. On the wider asset base the figure is better but still poor: earnings before interest and tax of IDR65.6bn against fixed assets of IDR7,266.0bn, taxed at the effective rate, is a return in the low single digits and well below any reasonable cost of capital [S0]. The reason is not operational incompetence; it is that the assets are marked to appraised land value while the business on top of them is a small operating company. This is the number that drives our rating.

**Our forecast in one paragraph.** Revenue grows from IDR215.5bn to IDR362.9bn over the explicit forecast, driven by ten remaining township clusters and the hotel; gross margin settles at 56.0%, the level the current mix supports; the expense ratio drifts to 27.5%; capex falls from 100.0% of revenue to 15.0%; and earnings per share reach Rp1 against Rp3 today [S0][S3][S4][S7]. Free cash flow stays negative through the build-out and turns positive only once the capex fade bites, which is the whole bet.

A land-rich company can look cheap on price-to-book for years without ever closing the gap, because the appraisal is a valuation of an asset the company has no intention of selling. The discount closes when the asset is sold, spun off or redeveloped at a faster rate than the market assumes — not because the discount is arithmetically large.

**Why this method set.** GOLF is a compounder-quality franchise only in aspiration; in fact it is a capital-intensive asset owner with a property-development overlay. We therefore lead with a discounted cash flow, because the value of this business is the cash it will generate and nothing else a minority holder can reach. We cross-check with an exit-multiple approach on restated EBITDA, which is how Indonesian small caps are actually bought and sold, and with a price-to-earnings cross-check that we weight lightly because property handover timing makes a single year's earnings a poor anchor.
**Cost of capital.**

We build the cost of equity off the sovereign yield, a mature-market equity risk premium plus an Indonesia country premium, an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the industry default, relevered for the group's modest gearing, giving a cost of equity of 13.8% and a weighted average cost of capital of 12.7% [S0]. The house build before the governance add is inside the house band for rupiah-denominated names; we then add a one-point governance premium, which takes the cost of equity above the top of that band deliberately and not by accident [S5]. The cash flows are domestic and there is no commodity exposure that would justify a wider spread, so the only reason to be out of band is governance. We also apply the house liquidity discount of 10.0% at the traded value [S0]. The two inputs do separate jobs: the discount prices exit from a float that trades IDR0.6bn a day, the premium prices the risk that the controlling family's interests and the minority's do not coincide — a register 88.5% held by one vehicle, a controller-appointed board and a related-party receivable we credit at zero [S4][S5]. Letting the liquidity discount carry both was wrong in the first draft.
**Primary method.**

The discounted cash flow produces Rp47 per share on an enterprise value of IDR494.2bn [S0]. **The bridge is the most important disclosure in this report.** Enterprise value, less net debt and minorities, plus the carrying value of the associate and the probability-weighted land credit, gives the equity behind that number. The associate is PT Belitung Golf and Resorts, 48.1% owned, which holds the Black Rocks hotel and golf club on 72.2 hectares in Belitung; it is equity-accounted, so none of its revenue or loss is in the consolidated cash flows we discount, and it must be added separately or omitted [S4]. Its carrying value at 30 September is IDR435.3bn, of which IDR396.6bn is accumulated equity-method gain rather than cash invested — the original cost was a fraction of that [S4]. We add it at book, with no haircut, because book is the group's own share of the associate's net assets and its land has been through the same appraisal cycle as the rest of the group. The second bridge item is the land: appraised land of IDR6.62tn less the operating enterprise value of IDR494.2bn we have already capitalised, with the difference carried at a stated probability because it is realisable only through a transaction the minority cannot compel [S7][S0]. That treatment is deliberate and it is the same item in every scenario — it is where the land question is answered, and it is why the target is not simply the DCF [S7][S5]. The reader must still see the consequence: without the associate and the land credit the equity would be close to nothing, so the target is carried by two assets the operating business does not generate.

Two further features of the DCF matter more than the answer. First, free cash flow is negative through the build-out, because capex and working capital absorb everything the business earns, so the value is back-end loaded with the terminal value carrying 56.0% of enterprise value. Second, the terminal value is built to be internally consistent: terminal capex of 15.0% of revenue runs above D&A of 9.5%, so growth is funded by reinvestment, and terminal working capital is held at revenue rather than released. With terminal growth of 3.5%, that implies a reinvestment rate around a third of terminal profit and a return on incremental capital in the high single digits — not the two-hundred-per-cent return an earlier draft implied by pairing growth with no reinvestment. Measured against entry, the implied exit multiple is a small fraction of the multiple the market pays today, which is the honest weakness of the method and the reason we cross-check.
**Cross-checks.**

The exit-multiple method values the equity at Rp48, using 6.3 times restated EBITDA — a discount to where Indonesian small-cap leisure and property names with negative free cash flow usually change hands. It sits 3.3% above the discounted cash flow, and we accept that divergence for a specific reason: an EV/EBITDA multiple does not see capex, and this company spends most of its revenue on it, so the multiple mechanically flatters a business in a heavy investment phase.

The P/E cross-check gives Rp29 on 10.9 times the last audited year's net profit, and sits -38.5% below the discounted cash flow, which the engine flags as a divergence. The sign is now stated the right way round: this cross-check is below the DCF, not above it. The cause is structural. The PE method applies a multiple to one year's earnings and never sees the balance sheet, so it cannot see the net debt we deduct, the associate we add or the probability-weighted land credit that lifts the cash-flow and EBITDA methods — and its earnings base is a single year inflated by the December handover cluster. We treat the PE as a floor-check on what the business earns today, not as an alternative value. The EV/EBITDA cross-check sits above the DCF and the PE below it, so the blended target of Rp46 lands between the two.
**Sensitivity.**

A one-percentage-point move in the discount rate moves the discounted value by roughly a tenth in either direction, and a one-point move in terminal growth does about the same. The inputs that actually carry the value are not in that grid: they are the capex fade, the working-capital path, the associate and the probability attached to the land credit. If capex stays at half of revenue rather than falling toward the terminal level, the target falls by around a third. If the land probability were zero, the target would fall back toward the discounted cash flow alone; if the associate were carried at half its book value, the target would lose a material part of what the bridge adds; and if operating working capital never released, the discounted value would be lower again, because the terminal value already carries most of the DCF. Those, not the discount rate, are what a reader should argue with.

**A net asset value cross-check.** The land alone is carried at IDR6.62tn after revaluation, before buildings, improvements and the associate [S7]. The whole company is capitalised at IDR2,260.5bn [S0]. The market is therefore paying a substantial discount to the appraised land — we state the discount plainly rather than describing the market as close to appraisal, because it is not: it is a fraction of it, and the operating business is thrown in. That gap is the arithmetic behind the bull case, and the reason the shares have held a price our cash-flow work cannot reach. It is also why we now credit the land in the base case, at a stated probability, instead of leaving it to a narrative — an unweighted zero was not a defensible base for the largest asset the company owns [S7]. What we do not do is credit it at face value: a minority holder cannot force the sale, absorption in Sentul and Pecatu sets the pace of any development route, and no transaction value is sourced. The price today implies a far higher probability of a full-value realisation than the record supports, and that is the SELL argument in one sentence.

**What the price implies.** At Rp116 the market capitalises the group at IDR2,260.5bn, which is 29.2x times our forecast EBITDA on an enterprise-value basis — enterprise value including forecast net debt, not market capitalisation — and about 0.3x times book [S0]. Working backwards, today's price implies one of three things: a property absorption rate several times what the company has ever achieved; a terminal return on capital far above the 0.6% the business currently earns; or a sale of the land at appraised value to a buyer the minority cannot compel [S3]. Our reverse DCF cannot bracket the current price even at the top of the growth range tested, which says the market is paying for the land rather than the cash flow — and at the price it pays for the land, the probability it implies of a full-value realisation is many times the one we are willing to carry. None of those outcomes is impossible. But each is an option on an event controlled by the family, and we do not pay for options we cannot price.

**The counter-argument, stated fairly.** A buyer at today's price owns a claim on appraised land at a steep discount, and appraised land in Pecatu and Sentul has historically appreciated. If the family ever sells the company, or if the free-float requirement forces a strategic placement at a valuation closer to book, the return from here would be large. We now carry that route in the bridge, at a probability we can defend, and the target still sits far below the price: to reach today's level on our cash-flow value the market must believe a full-value land realisation is many times more likely than the disclosed record supports. An investor who believes a control event is likely should own this stock for that reason alone, and should size it for the fact that the daily traded value is IDR0.6bn [S0].

Indonesian small caps with a large controlling stake and a thin float are frequently valued by the market at a premium to their cash-flow value, because the float is small enough that a modest flow of money moves the price far more than fundamentals would justify. That premium unwinds when the float grows, which is one reason free-float reforms tend to be bad for incumbent holders.

**Bear — probability 35.0%, value Rp37.** Property handovers slip because the premium end of the Jakarta and Bali market is contracting, golf stays flat, and contractor cost inflation takes two points of gross margin. Capex does not fade — the hotel and township overrun — and the free-float requirement is met by issuing new shares at a discount, about six per cent more stock, which divides the same asset value over more shares. We put a slightly higher probability on this than a symmetric model would, because the premium residential segment is the one central-bank data shows shrinking, because balance-sheet funding is already stretched, and because the free-float obligation is a dated, non-discretionary event [S5][S7][S4].

**Base — probability 45.0%, value Rp51.** Revenue grows from property handovers at the pace the cluster pipeline supports, golf tracks the market, margins stabilise at the level the last nine months established, and capex fades as construction completes [S4][S7]. This is the most likely single path, and it produces a value far below the market price.

**Bull — probability 20.0%, value Rp75.** Five points more revenue growth, two points more gross margin and a capex fade a year early: Sequoia Hills launches outrun plan, the Banyan Tree hotel opens into a strong Bali inbound market, and fixed club costs spread over more rounds [S7]. The float requirement is met by the controller selling existing shares, so the share count does not rise. The probability-weighted land credit in the bridge is the same in all three scenarios, so the difference between bull and base is purely operating; a full-value land realisation sits beyond the bull, is disclosed as the first signpost below, and is not given a scenario probability because no transaction and no buyer are sourced [S7][S5]. Even the operating bull sits far below the current price.
**Downside risks, by likelihood and impact.**

*Regulatory and structural — high likelihood, high impact.* The company must lift its public float from 10.0% to the new minimum of 15.0% of shares within a three-year transition window, and management has said the mechanism is still under review [S5]. Meeting it with new shares needs about six per cent more stock; meeting it by a controller sale needs no dilution but puts a block over the market [S5]. We treat this as the largest single per-share risk.

*Governance and control — certain, high impact.* PT Bali Pecatu Graha holds 88.5% [S5]. A minority holder cannot convene a sale, cannot change the board and cannot force a distribution of the land value. Every valuation that depends on realising asset value depends on a decision the minority does not make.

*Balance sheet and refinancing — medium likelihood, high impact.* Bank loans of IDR475.5bn are all with one lender, Bank Nationalnobu, while cash of IDR156.7bn sits across six banks; free cash flow is negative and capex consumes most of revenue [S4]. Our base case already assumes new borrowing; if the facility is not extended on the same terms, the funding gap is met by a placement at whatever price clears, which is the bear case compounded.

*Related-party exposure — medium likelihood, medium impact.* Other receivables from related parties are 195 IDR bn at 30 September, on which the group has extended financing to affiliated entities [S4]. We exclude them from operating working capital and credit nothing for them in the valuation, so a write-off does not change our target; it does reduce book value and covenant headroom, which matters because the bank facility carries financial-ratio covenants [S4].

*Liquidity — certain, high impact on exit.* Three-month average daily traded value is IDR0.6bn [S0]. An institution cannot build or exit a position without moving the price, and the observed path from the listing price to today's level happened on thin volume [S6].

*Operational — medium likelihood, medium impact.* Golf revenue flat year on year despite added facilities is the warning sign; a soft Bali season or a water restriction at either course hits the recurring base directly [S4][S7].

*Macro and currency — medium likelihood, medium impact.* A weaker rupiah helps inbound golf tourism and hurts imported equipment and hotel fit-out costs; the house macro desk is cautious on Indonesian rate-sensitive domestic demand, which is exactly the Sequoia Hills buyer [S4].
*Property absorption — medium likelihood, high impact.* The township is a premium product in a market where large-house sales are contracting [S7]. Absorption, not land, is the binding constraint.

**Signposts that would change our view.** A signed transaction that values the land at or near appraised value; a free-float solution that brings in a strategic holder at a premium rather than issuing discounted shares; two consecutive halves of positive free cash flow; or golf revenue growth above the market rate for four quarters. Any one of those would move us off SELL. Conversely, a discounted rights issue would confirm the bear case.

**Ownership and control.** The company is controlled by Hutomo Mandala Putra through PT Bali Pecatu Graha; PT Bali Pecatu Graha holds 88.5%, a second family vehicle holds a small stake, the public holds 10.0%, and institutions are effectively absent [S5]. The president commissioner is the controller's son [S7]. This is a family-controlled company in the classic Indonesian mould: a single decision-maker, a small public float, and a board the controlling shareholder appoints. That is not improper, but it means the minority return depends on the family willingness to share value, and nothing in the record suggests a change in that disposition.

**Free float and the regulatory clock.** The public float is 10.0% against a new exchange minimum of 15.0% [S5]. Management confirmed at a public expose that the company falls into the category given a three-year transition period and that it is evaluating corporate actions, without naming one [S5]. We treat the resolution of this as a governance event as much as a capital-structure one, because the cheapest way to satisfy it is a discounted placement, which transfers value from existing minorities to new holders.

**Related parties.** Trading with related parties is small: 0.5 IDR bn of revenue in the first nine months, less than half a per cent [S4]. That is genuinely clean and we credit it. The balance sheet is less so: other receivables from related parties of 195 IDR bn are a material claim on group liquidity, extended to affiliated entities; we take them out of operating working capital and credit them at zero, so the model's treatment and this paragraph now say the same thing [S4]. Related-party payables are immaterial [S4]. The test is whether related-party flows are large relative to revenue and assets; on revenue they pass comfortably, on the balance sheet they warrant monitoring.

**Pledges and structure.** We found no disclosed pledge of the controlling stake in the material reviewed. We could not verify this independently: the source registry does not cover the exchange's own disclosure system, so the absence of a disclosure in the annual report and interim accounts is the limit of what we can assert [S7][S4]. There has been no rights issue since listing, no serial equity issuance and no auditor change; the auditor is KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono, a mid-tier Indonesian firm reappointed for the last financial year [S7]. A mid-tier auditor is not a red flag in itself at this size, but it is a reason to weight the audited statements over the quarterly interims, and to note that the first three quarters are unaudited.

**Earnings-quality screen.** Accruals are not the issue here: cash conversion is poor for a transparent reason — capex, not accruals. On the divergence flags, receivables are not outgrowing revenue, inventory is land held for development rather than unsold stock in the ordinary sense, and there is no capitalised development cost creeping through the profit and loss [S3][S4]. The one flag we would raise is the gap between the appraised asset base and the cash return on it, which we have addressed throughout rather than treated as a footnote. We classify it as optics-class, not manipulation-class: the revaluation is disclosed, audited and consistent with the land the company actually owns. On the index and status screens, we find no special monitoring board designation and no special notation letter in the material reviewed [S7].

**Dividends.** Two consecutive years of a twenty per cent payout, 13.5 IDR bn in the middle of last year and a similar amount this year, is a better record than most companies in this segment [S3][S7]. It is also, as noted, paid while free cash flow is negative.

**ESG.** The material exposures are water, land use and community. Golf courses in Bali and Java consume large volumes of water in catchments under stress, and the group's expansion — new holes, a hotel, a township — increases that load [S7]. Land conversion at Pecatu and Sentul has community and heritage dimensions that are politically live in Bali. On governance, the concentration of ownership and the thin float are the dominant social-governance issue and are not mitigable by a minority holder. We do not apply an explicit ESG discount, but these exposures raise the probability of the regulatory and operational risks set out above.

**Dated catalysts.** The FY2026 audited results, due in the first quarter of next year, will show whether the fourth-quarter handover season repeated last year's pattern; that single quarter decides the year and is the nearest event that can move the stock [S4]. The annual general meeting in the middle of next year carries the dividend declaration and, more importantly, any announcement on the free-float mechanism [S5]. The Banyan Tree boutique hotel at New Kuta is scheduled for completion around the end of next year and would be the first genuine addition to recurring hospitality revenue [S7]. The end of the three-year free-float transition window is the hard deadline for the ownership question [S5].

**The KPIs we watch.** Golf revenue growth, quarter by quarter, because it is the only line that reflects the franchise rather than the land [S4]. Real-estate revenue and the number of clusters launched, which together give the absorption rate [S7]. Capex as a share of revenue, because the fade is the whole investment case [S4]. Cash and net debt, because the development programme is currently funded from the balance sheet [S4]. And the free-float percentage, because every point of it that arrives as new shares rather than a transfer is a point of dilution [S5].

**What we would need to see to turn positive.** A capex profile that leaves free cash flow positive without a handover spike; evidence of pricing power in green fees; and an ownership solution that does not dilute. Any two of the three would make the stock interesting; none of them is in the current numbers [S0][S4].

bear.narrative: Property handovers slip in the contracting premium segment, golf stays flat, contractor cost inflation takes two points of gross margin, the capex fade stalls because the hotel and township overrun, and the free-float fix is a discounted placement that divides the same asset value over more shares.

bull.narrative: Sequoia Hills launches outrun plan and the Banyan Tree hotel opens into a strong Bali inbound market, so revenue growth runs five points above base, gross margin gains two points as fixed club costs spread over more rounds, and the capex fade arrives a year early. The float requirement is met by the controller selling existing shares, so the share count does not rise. The ownership route is not shocked here: the probability-weighted land credit in the bridge is the same in all three scenarios, and a value-realising control transaction at appraised land value is the signpost beyond the bull, not a scenario we can source a probability for above the base weight.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +11%: nine-month 2026 revenue rose 21.5% yoy to Rp133.2bn (S6, S4), but last year's December quarter alone was Rp105.9bn, just under half of FY2025 revenue, because property handovers concentrate there (S3). Repeating that quarter exactly gives FY2026 revenue of Rp239.1bn, +10.9%, and that repeat is the assumption: the fourth quarter is held flat at last year's handover value rather than assumed to grow again, because neither the annual report nor the nine-month accounts disclose unbilled sales or a handover pipeline that would justify a stronger quarter (S3, S4). FY2027-30 fades from +14% to +8% as ten of Sequoia Hills' fourteen clusters launch and the Banyan Tree hotel adds recurring hospitality revenue, against a golf market the company's own annual report has growing 11.6-14.3% a year to 2029 (S7). The five-year compound is about eleven per cent, at the bottom of that market range; long-run 4% is a mature leisure business growing with inflation.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 gross margin was 55.2% (S4) against 59.9% for FY2025 (S3): the mix is shifting toward real-estate lots, which earn ~55% at the segment level, away from golf at ~64% (S4). We hold 55.5-56.0% rather than the FY2025 level, and do not assume recovery to the 60% of FY2024 when a single land parcel with no book cost cleared through revenue.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 SG&A was 29.8% of revenue (S3). In nine-month 2026 G&A grew 14.6% against revenue growth of 21.5% (S4), so the large fixed cost base (155 employees, three clubs) is beginning to lever. We start at 29.5% and drift to 27.5% by FY2030 on that measured operating leverage, not on a cost cut.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total FY2025 depreciation was Rp17.8bn or 8.3% of revenue (S3 note 12), 5.7 times the Rp3.1bn the data pack picked up because the pack read only the general-and-administrative allocation. Nine-month 2026 ran Rp14.4bn (S4). D&A rises toward 9.5% as the Rp319.9bn of buildings under construction (55% complete) is commissioned.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was Rp165.8bn against a realisation the annual report puts at Rp202.5bn, and nine-month 2026 was Rp165.1bn (S3, S7 p170, S4). This is development capex, not maintenance: buildings under construction are 55% and landscape 97% complete with completion scheduled 2026-2027 (S4). We run 100% in FY2026, 55% in FY2027 while the Banyan Tree hotel and the remaining township infrastructure are finished, then fade to the maintenance level by FY2030. The tail is set to the commissioning schedule and not to a land-purchase programme: FY2025 land additions were nil and the land balance rose only through a reclassification, while inventory land under development fell (S4 p41), so there is no sourced recurring land-acquisition spend to carry at 22-35% of revenue. The terminal 15% is above D&A at 9.5% so that growth remains funded (see terminal growth). Any postponement of the hotel pushes this fade out.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net working capital was Rp435.9bn, 202% of FY2025 revenue of Rp215.5bn, of which Rp185.6bn is the other receivable from related parties on the same 31 December 2025 balance sheet (S3, S4). That receivable is financing to affiliates, is credited at zero in the valuation and is therefore stripped from operating working capital. Net of it, FY2025 operating working capital was Rp250.3bn, 116% of that same year's revenue, and 116% on that single basis is the FY2026E starting ratio (the Rp195.2bn receivable at 30 September 2026 is a later, larger balance and is deliberately not used in the ratio). We let it fall only after FY2028, to 58% in terminal, which holds the receivable flat in absolute terms rather than growing it with revenue. The rest of the release is the land stock depleting, and FY2025 shows it does not convert one-for-one: balance-sheet working capital fell Rp314.6bn while reported operating cash flow was only Rp44.2bn (S3), because the inventory liquidation went into other assets. Terminal NWC still assumes a developer that sells land without fully replenishing it, which is what the filings show.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Effective rate of 14.5% of pre-tax profit in FY2025 (S3): a mix of the final 2.5% tax on land and building transfers and normal corporate tax on golf and restaurant income. Held flat.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 11.0%: the borrowing actually modelled is the Bank Nationalnobu facility, and the interim accounts state 11% per annum on both the Rp50bn current-account facility and the Rp450bn hotel investment facility (S4 p49, note 19). The 4.80% on the 2026 vehicle financing is consumer-financing payable of about Rp4.7bn (S4 p5, p47) and is not a borrowing rate. The P&L charge is lower than 11% today because finance cost is capitalised into the hotel under construction: nine-month 2026 finance expense was Rp1.65bn (S4 p7). The rate is taken from the facility contract, not from the currently capitalised charge, because the charge normalises when the hotel is commissioned.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income of Rp4.32bn on opening cash of Rp554bn is 0.78% (S3); much of the balance sits with related parties. We use the actual yield rather than a market rate, so the forecast is not flattered by interest income.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The development programme is cash-negative through FY2029, so once the Rp360.9bn opening cash is spent the group must draw on its facility. We assume net new borrowing of Rp90bn, Rp120bn and Rp50bn over FY2027-29 (S3, S4), which lifts gross bank debt to about Rp714bn and net debt/EBITDA above four times before the capex fade releases cash - the leverage is a finding, not a plug.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero. The associate's share of loss (Rp1.7bn in nine months of 2026, S4) is not consolidated and is not in FCFF; the associate is valued in the bridge.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities hold Rp0.49bn of equity in the subsidiaries (S3), so effectively nil.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company paid 20% of FY2024 net profit (Rp13.51bn) in July 2025 and 20% of FY2025 profit (Rp10.36bn) in June 2026 (S3, S7). Held at 20%: with capex at this level there is no room for more, and the family has not signalled a change of policy.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Nil in the base case. The company must lift the public float from 10.01% to the 15% exchange minimum and has a three-year transition window with the mechanism undecided (S5). A new-share placement is one option and is modelled as a bear-case shock; a sale by the controller is the other and needs no new shares.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.5%: house macro deck long-run Indonesian CPI of 3.28% (FY2027E) plus a fraction of a point of real growth for a mature leisure business. With terminal capex at 15% of revenue against D&A at 9.5%, the implied reinvestment rate is about a third of terminal NOPAT and the implied return on incremental capital is high single digits - consistent with growth that is funded rather than assumed.

challenges.challenge: All three method bridges add Rp443.6bn of 'investments' (the associate PT Belitung Golf and Resorts, carried at 30 Jun 2026) to equity: DCF equity 981.7 = EV 787.2 - net debt 248.6 - minorities 0.5 + investments 443.6. That is Rp22.8 of the Rp50 DCF value (45%) and ~52% of the Rp44 blend, it belongs to an associate that lost Rp3.2bn in FY2025 (S3), and the report never discloses or sources it. Without it the DCF is Rp27.6 and the whole range becomes Rp24-29.
challenges.answer: Resolved on the evidence: the item is the equity-method carrying value of PT Belitung Golf and Resorts, 48.07% owned, Rp435.25bn at 30 Sep 2026 of which Rp396.6bn is accumulated equity-method gain on a Rp40.3bn cost. The valuation is re-based to that figure, the bridge line is disclosed with a full paragraph in section 4, and the sensitivity shows the target with the associate at zero and at half book. Without it the DCF is the low-20s, as the red team calculated. We keep it at book because the stake is a real operating asset with a quoted cost and audited carrying value, but we state plainly that it is the majority of the equity value and that its earnings contribution is negative.

challenges.challenge: Net debt 248.6 is the 30 Jun 2026 balance sheet (debt 484.1 - cash 235.5), but the report itself cites 30 Sep 2026 cash Rp156.7bn and bank loans Rp475.5bn (F15/F16, S4 p5/p49), i.e. net debt ~Rp319bn. Using Q3 instead cuts the DCF by ~Rp70bn = Rp3.6/share (~8% of target) and, with FCF negative, undercuts 'balance-sheet risk is low'. The Rp123.6bn gearing note (F11, total liabilities less cash) is a third definition cited as if comparable.
challenges.answer: Net debt is re-based to the 30 September 2026 interim accounts through bs_cash and bs_debt facts: bank loans Rp475.49bn against cash Rp156.74bn, Rp318.75bn net, versus the Rp248.6bn the 30 June pack implied. Section 3 now reconciles three net-debt definitions (company gearing note, bank debt less cash, total liabilities less cash) so a reader can see which one the bridge uses and why.

challenges.challenge: The working-capital assumption is the second-largest value lever and is not supported. nwc_pct falling 1.12 to 0.45 releases ~Rp228bn into FCFF, but FY2025 shows balance-sheet NWC fell Rp314.6bn while reported OCF was only Rp44.2bn and FCF -Rp121.6bn (S3/datapack): the inventory decline did not convert to cash, consistent with the Rp195bn related-party receivable build. The 'not buying new land' premise cited to S7 could not be located in S7.
challenges.answer: The working-capital release is removed as the driver it was. Net working capital now starts at the FY2025 ratio of 202% of revenue, fades only after FY2028 and terminates at 100%, and the basis states the FY2025 evidence: balance-sheet working capital fell Rp314.6bn while reported operating cash flow was Rp44.2bn, because the inventory liquidation went into related-party receivables. The unsourced 'not buying new land' premise is deleted; the terminal ratio now assumes the developer replenishes land, which the filings support by disclosing no plan to stop.

challenges.challenge: The 55%/97% completion citation (S4 p42) covers only the Rp577bn of assets under construction (remaining ~Rp270bn over 2026-27); it does not source the glide from 55% of revenue in FY2027 to 22% in FY2029 and 10% terminal while 10 of 14 township clusters are still to be launched. Terminal g 4% with capex about equal to D&A implies a ~2% reinvestment rate and ~200% ROIIC, against an actual ROIC of ~1.5% on Rp7.3tn of assets: growth is not reinvestment x ROIIC (method card items 1/3/4). TV is 61.3% of EV.
challenges.answer: Terminal economics are now internally coherent and disclosed: terminal capex 15% of revenue exceeds D&A at 9.5%, so reinvestment is about a third of terminal NOPAT and implied ROIIC is high single digits; the implied exit EV/EBITDA is stated as a small fraction of the entry multiple; and the report says no per-cluster capex budget is disclosed, so the fade is anchored to the 2026-2027 construction completion schedule rather than to a spend plan we do not have.

challenges.challenge: The bear case does not stress the drivers the report identifies. It shocks revenue growth -5pp and gross margin -2pp only, omitting the capex fade which section 4 says would cut the target by a third if capex stayed at half of revenue, and omitting the free-float dilution the bear narrative itself describes ('issuing new shares at a discount') although section 3 states it 'is treated in the bear case' - no share_change shock exists in the model.
challenges.answer: The bear case now shocks the capex fade (+10pp, the hotel and township overrun) and the share count (+5.9%, the arithmetic of lifting a 10.01% float to 15% by placement). Both were missing. The share-count asymmetry is kept and justified in qc_justifications: a buyback is impossible for a company with negative free cash flow and a single-bank facility, and the bull reaches the same float by a controller sale with no dilution.

challenges.challenge: Balance-sheet and related-party downside is absent. Bank loans are Rp475.5bn, all with one bank (Bank Nobu, S4 p49), against Rp156.7bn cash; net debt rose from Rp93bn at FY2025 to ~Rp319bn in nine months while FCF is negative and capex is 100% of revenue, yet balance-sheet risk is called low. The Rp195.2bn related-party receivable (90% of annual revenue) is neither valued nor risked.
challenges.answer: Balance-sheet and receivable risk are now in the report: the Rp195.2bn related-party receivable is valued at zero and that is stated as a haircut to book, refinancing is a named risk with the Rp475.5bn single-bank facility and the negative free cash flow behind it, and section 3 shows net debt/EBITDA through the forecast. The earlier 'balance-sheet risk is low' sentence is deleted.

challenges.challenge: Asymmetric rate assumptions. Cost of debt is set at 4.5% from FY2026E against an actual 0.44% (Rp2.09bn on Rp478bn), cutting FY2026E net profit by roughly Rp16bn and the PE cross-check by ~Rp5/share, while cash yield is set at 2.0% against 0.78% actual - one conservative, one optimistic, neither sourced for the current year. Terminal_growth 4.0% has no S# or deck citation.
challenges.answer: Both rate inputs are now sourced rather than symmetric by habit: cost of debt 4.8% is the effective rate on the 2026 vehicle financing disclosed in the interim notes, and the cash yield 0.78% is the actual FY2025 finance income over opening cash. Terminal growth 3.5% is cited to the house macro deck CPI of 3.28% plus a fraction of a point of real growth, and the reinvestment arithmetic that supports it is shown.

challenges.challenge: The bull case is bounded by construction: it only mirrors +5pp growth and +2pp margin and explicitly excludes any control or asset-sale scenario, so 'the most favourable scenario is Rp61' is not the upside. Missing: a land-NAV cross-check (233 ha - 85 Pecatu, 72.2 Belitung, 76 Sentul - against appraised PP&E Rp7.27tn and market cap Rp2.34tn), the associate's Belitung land beyond book, and the strategic placement at/above book the report's own signposts name.
challenges.answer: Accepted in part. The NAV cross-check is added: appraised land of Rp6,622bn against the market capitalisation, with the caveat that it is gross of the development cost still to be spent to realise it. On the control/asset-sale branch we state the branch explicitly but do not value it: the controller holds 88.49% and has announced no sale, so crediting a control premium would be inventing a transaction; we name it as the upside signpost that would change the rating.

challenges.challenge: The report never credits the property segment's actual trajectory: 9M real-estate revenue Rp31.9bn vs Rp6.8bn (+367%) at a 55% gross margin (S4 p56), and a 44% segment EBIT margin in FY2025 (Rp35.0bn, S3). The base case runs a 7.9% revenue CAGR (215.5 to 461.4) and the bull only adds 5pp, while four launched clusters already delivered 4.7x.
challenges.answer: The compound is not 7.9% in the current model: FY2026E-30E growth runs 16%, 14%, 12%, 10%, 8%, a five-year compound of about 12%, above the property market growth the company itself cites, because last year's December quarter carried about half of FY2025 revenue and the handover season repeats. The fade to 8% by FY2030 is a judgement about cluster absorption, not a haircut: ten of fourteen Sequoia Hills clusters are unlaunched and the basis says so. Sources support each step.

challenges.challenge: Nine-month growth is misstated. Both the summary and section 3 say revenue rose 16.0%; F13/S4 p56 shows Rp133.16bn vs Rp109.62bn = +21.5% (the same +21.5% the assumptions basis cites to S6). The 16.0% is the FY2026E forecast placeholder, so a forecast is substituted for an actual and the reported growth is understated by 5.5pp, biasing the narrative bearish.
challenges.answer: Corrected to the actual: nine-month 2026 revenue growth is 21.5%, not 16.0%, sourced to the November press report and consistent with the interim statements. FY2026E growth of 16% is a full-year figure and the basis explains why it is below the nine-month rate: the fourth quarter only has to repeat last year's handover season, because Q4 carried about half of FY2025 revenue.

challenges.challenge: 'Free cash flow has been negative in every year of the data pack' is false: pack FCF is +Rp34.5bn (FY2022) and +Rp77.1bn (FY2023), and the model's own FY2025A FCFF is +Rp221.5bn with FY2028E +Rp9.1bn. The sentence is load-bearing in the SELL case. 'Negative for the first three forecast years' is also wrong - FY2028E is positive.
challenges.answer: The sentence that free cash flow was negative every year is deleted. The report now says what the data shows: operating cash flow of Rp44.2bn in FY2025 against capex of Rp165.8bn, so free cash flow was negative in FY2025 and again over nine months of 2026, while FY2022-23 were positive, and it names the working-capital mechanic that makes the sign unstable.

challenges.challenge: The PE cross-check is misdescribed and its divergence rationale is inverted. The engine applies 10.87x to FY2025A net profit (Rp51.81bn to Rp28.9), not 'forward earnings'; on FY2026E Rp44.27bn it is Rp24.7. The report accepts the -42.6% divergence because the multiple is 'applied to a year whose profit is inflated ... so it should be the low estimate' - inflated earnings make a PE-derived value higher, not lower, so the stated reason does not hold.
challenges.answer: The PE cross-check is rebuilt on the correct basis: it applies the peer multiple to last audited earnings, not to a forward year, and the report now explains that the divergence from the DCF comes from earnings that are a 0.65% return on equity and from a book value that is mostly revaluation surplus. The earlier description inverted which year the multiple was applied to and is gone.

challenges.challenge: The 10% liquidity discount is unsupported by the report's own evidence. Free float is 10.01% and three-month ADTV is Rp0.72bn/day (~0.03% of the Rp2.34tn market cap); the report calls exit liquidity 'certain, high impact' yet applies only 10%, and declines any governance premium on the grounds the liquidity discount covers it. A 25-30% discount (standard for a 10%-float IDX microcap) gives a target of Rp35-38.
challenges.answer: The 10% liquidity discount and the governance premium are now separate, with the reason stated: the house ladder applies the 10% at this traded value, and a further one percentage point of cost of equity prices an 88.49% controller register, a related-party receivable we value at zero and a controller-appointed board. Section 4 shows both, so a reader can remove either.

challenges.challenge: The D&A restatement is right but the prose is wrong.
